summary: For ages 5–7, teach 'living things' vocabulary as language children USE to give reasons, not a list to recite. Children acquire and apply the words living, dead, never been alive, and the life-process words (movement, nutrition/feeding, growth, reproduction, sensitivity, excretion) by binding each word to a visible feature on a real organism and by sorting real and pictured objects into three bins while stating a spoken reason. Deliberately include tricky contrast cases (fire, a wind-up toy, a seed, a shell, a fallen leaf) to surface and challenge the intuitive 'it moves so it's alive' rule, and attach each life-process word to a PLANT as well as an animal so the vocabulary generalises beyond moving animals. The UK KS1 Y2 statutory focus is comparing living / dead / never-been-alive; the seven life processes (MRS GREN) are supporting, non-statutory language in England, and this lesson uses six of them, leaving out respiration (the R) as too abstract for this age. Developmentally, early KS1 children equate living with movement; surfacing fire-is-alive and plant-is-not-alive errors is the point of the lesson, not a failure.
misconceptions: 'It moves so it's alive' — children over-generalise movement, judging fire, the sun, a clock or a boat to be living.
'Plants (and seeds and fungi) are not alive' — because they are not obviously active or moving; seeds especially are judged non-living.
Confusing 'dead' with 'never been alive' — e.g. treating a rock and a fallen leaf as the same category.
Attributing intentional, animal-like purpose to plants (a plant grows to the light because it 'wants' to), rather than describing sensitivity as a response.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal 'what makes it living' scene
steps: Look at a single rich scene containing a tree, a bird, a child, a seed, a fallen leaf, a rock, a toy, and a campfire.

Tap or point to a life-process word (movement, nutrition/feeding, growth, reproduction, sensitivity) and find the evidence for it on the organism: tap 'growth' and a seedling thickens and adds a leaf; tap 'nutrition' and the tree's roots take in water while its leaves use sunlight to make the tree's food, and the bird pecks a berry; tap 'reproduction' and the tree's seeds highlight; tap 'sensitivity' and the leaves slowly turn toward the light (shown speeded up) and the bird turns its head to a sound.

Tap 'movement' expecting only the bird to respond, and notice that parts of the tree move too, shown speeded up: its leaves slowly turn toward the light and its flowers open and close — a plant moves parts of itself even though it cannot walk about.
For each word, say it aloud applied to BOTH a plant and an animal (e.g. 'the tree grows and the bird grows').

Open the campfire flap: 'The fire flickers and grows — is it living?' and talk through how it differs from living things: it burns fuel but does not feed and use food to build its own body, it cannot sense and respond to its surroundings, and it can spread but does not have young that grow up.
activities.insight: Each life-process word maps to a feature you can see on a real organism, and plants show these processes too — so movement alone does not decide what is living.

activities.title: Three-way sort with a spoken reason
steps: Sort real and pictured objects into three bins: living / dead / never been alive.
Start with familiar organisms from the child's own environment (a growing plant, a pet, a person) before moving to edge cases.
Include the tricky contrast cases: fire, a wind-up or toy dog, a seed, a shell, a fallen leaf, a wooden chair, a rock.
After placing each object, pick the life-process word that justifies the choice and say the reason aloud ('the shell is dead because it was part of a living snail').
For 'dead' versus 'never been alive', trace the material to its origin: wood came from a tree and wool from a sheep (dead / once alive), while plastic and metal were never alive.
activities.insight: Deciding living / dead / never-been-alive means checking several life processes and, for non-living things, whether they were ever part of something alive — not just whether they move.

activities.title: Word-to-picture matching and a check sort
steps: Match each clearly observable life-process word (movement, nutrition, growth, reproduction, sensitivity) to a photograph that shows it, and treat excretion as 'getting rid of waste' with an everyday example (such as an animal producing waste) rather than requiring an unambiguous single photo.
Sort six items into living / dead / never been alive, with fire and a seed included as deliberate contrast items.
For each decision, name a life-process word that justifies it.
activities.insight: I can recognise which word names which life process and use the right word when I classify an object.

activities.title: 'Is it alive?' questioning exchange
steps: Respond when a curious character holds up an object and asks 'Is it alive? Why?', naming a life-process reason.

Answer the probes when the character pushes back: 'But a car moves — is a car alive?', 'The river moves too — but does it grow, feed or reproduce?', and 'A toy robot walks and beeps — is it living? Why not?'
Give two life-process words that show a sunflower is alive, and say why a wooden chair is dead (once alive) rather than never alive.
activities.insight: Movement alone does not make something living; I must check the other life processes to decide and explain, so I do not simply swap 'it moves' for one other single rule.

checkQuestion: Tell me whether each of these is living, dead, or never been alive, and use a 'life process' word to say why: a sunflower growing in a pot, a wooden chair, and a car driving down the road.
checkAnswer: The sunflower is living — it grows, needs nutrition and reproduces (life-process words). The wooden chair was once part of a living tree, so it is dead (once alive). The car has never been alive — it moves, but it doesn't grow, feed or reproduce; movement alone doesn't make something living. The child gives a life-process reason for each.
